title: Math & Technical Notes Blog — Complete Workflow
text:
A start-to-finish process for launching, publishing, and sustaining an English-language blog showcasing your pure & applied mathematics work. Built on Quarto (static site generator) + Git + GitHub Pages.










Need
Quarto delivers




LaTeX math
Native $...$ / $$...$$ via MathJax/KaTeX, no setup


Theorems, proofs, lemmas
.theorem/.proof callout environments with auto-numbering


Citations / bibliography
BibTeX (references.bib) + auto-formatted reference list


Executable code
Embed & run Python/R/Julia, show output and figures inline


Cross-references
@eq-..., @thm-..., @fig-... auto-numbered links


Cost
Free hosting on GitHub Pages or Netlify


Portability
Plain .qmd (Markdown) files in Git — you own everything



Output is a fast static site. No database, no server to maintain.




Decide these before writing a line of code. They shape every later choice.

Audience. Who reads this? (Graduate peers, recruiters/grad-admissions, your future self, the general math-curious.) You picked English-first → optimize for an international/academic audience and citability.
Scope & pillars. Pick 3–4 recurring categories so the blog reads as coherent, not random. Suggested for pure + applied math:

Pure: analysis, algebra, topology, number theory
Applied: numerical methods, optimization, probability/statistics, PDEs
Meta: paper reviews, study notes, problem sets / solutions

The promise. One sentence describing what a reader reliably gets. E.g. “Self-contained notes that derive results from first principles, with runnable code where it helps intuition.”
Cadence. Be honest. One solid post every 2 weeks beats five then silence. Set a sustainable rhythm now.
Name & domain. Short, memorable, ideally your name or a math handle. Reserve the matching GitHub repo and (optionally) a .com/.dev/.xyz domain.

Deliverable: a half-page note (audience, pillars, promise, cadence, name).




This repo already contains the scaffold. Steps:

Install Quarto (see README.md) and a recent Python (for code cells).
quarto preview to see it live with hot reload.
Edit _quarto.yml: set title, your name, social links, repo URL.
Personalize about.qmd (bio, research interests, CV link, contact).
Replace the sample posts in posts/ once you understand the pattern.
Tune look in styles.css (or swap the Bootstrap theme in _quarto.yml).

Definition of done: site builds clean, homepage lists posts, About reads as you.




A consistent pipeline is what makes a blog survive past post #3.

Capture. Keep a running ideas.md of post seeds (a theorem you re-derived, a paper you read, a problem you solved). Never start from a blank page.
Draft in a branch. git checkout -b post/spectral-theorem. New folder posts/<slug>/index.qmd.
Front matter. Title, date, categories, description, draft: true until ready.
Write math-first. State the result, then build to it. Use theorem/proof callouts. Define notation once. Add a figure or runnable snippet only where it earns its place.
Cite. Add sources to references.bib, reference with [@key].
Self-review checklist (see Phase 6).
Render & proof locally. Check every equation renders, every cross-ref resolves, code runs top-to-bottom in a clean kernel.
Flip draft: false, merge, push. CI (or quarto publish) deploys.

Target: idea → published in 2–4 focused sessions per post.





Deploy. GitHub Pages via quarto publish gh-pages, or connect the repo to Netlify for auto-deploy on push. (Full commands in README.md.)
Custom domain (optional but worth it for credibility): point a CNAME at GitHub Pages / Netlify.
SEO baseline. Each post needs a description, descriptive title, and image for social cards. Quarto generates sitemap + Open Graph tags when site-url is set.
Make it citable. Add a “How to cite” block to substantial posts; consider archiving milestone notes to Zenodo for a DOI.
Share intentionally. Post to the venues your audience actually reads: relevant subreddits (r/math, r/mathematics), Mathstodon, Hacker News for applied/CS-adjacent pieces, your university/department channels, LinkedIn for the recruiter audience. Don’t spam — share the ones genuinely worth others’ time.
RSS. Quarto emits a feed automatically; mention it so regular readers can subscribe.






Content calendar. Keep ideas.md ranked; schedule the next 2–3 posts.
Series. Group related notes (e.g. a “Functional Analysis notes” series) — series convert one-time readers into followers.
Engagement. Enable comments (giscus = GitHub Discussions, spam-free and fits the audience).
Analytics. Add privacy-friendly analytics (Plausible, or GoatCounter free) to learn what resonates. Avoid vanity-metric chasing.
Refactor old posts. Fix errors readers flag; mathematics blogs gain authority from being correct and maintained.
Review cadence quarterly. What got traction? What drained time for no return? Adjust pillars.





Run this before every publish. Correctness is the whole reputation of a math blog.

Every claim is either proved, cited, or explicitly flagged as conjecture/intuition.
Notation is defined before use; consistent throughout.
All equations render; numbered ones are referenced.
Proofs have no silent gaps (“clearly”, “obviously” earn scrutiny).
Code runs end-to-end in a fresh kernel and outputs match the prose.
description + title are accurate and search-friendly.
Links and citations resolve.
A non-expert can follow the motivation, even if not every step.












When
Milestone




Day 1
Phase 1 positioning + repo/domain reserved


Day 2
Site builds locally, About done, deployed to a live URL


Week 1
First real post published (start with something you already know cold)


Weeks 2–8
Establish cadence: 1 post / 1–2 weeks; refine template


Quarter 1
5–8 posts, comments + analytics live, 1 series started



Start small and real. Your first post should be something you can already explain without notes — that gets you to “published” fastest and builds momentum.

title: About
text:
I’m Xihan Fang, a mathematics student interested in the connection between pure mathematical theory, computational methods, and quantitative modelling.
My academic interests lie across topology, analysis, network science, stochastic processes, optimization, and quantitative finance. I use this site as a long-term archive for mathematical notes, technical derivations, paper reviews, and reproducible computational experiments.

title: About
text:
Research interests

Pure mathematics: topology, analysis, algebra, and mathematical structures.
Applied mathematics: network science, stochastic processes, optimization, and numerical methods.
Quantitative finance: market modelling, risk, statistical learning, and systematic research workflows.
Mathematical modelling: model formulation, parameter estimation, sensitivity analysis, and computational verification.

title: About
text:
What you’ll find here
This blog collects notes and projects written with three aims:

to make definitions, theorems, and proofs precise enough to revisit later;
to connect abstract mathematics with computational and modelling problems;
to document reproducible calculations, simulations, and research ideas.

Some posts are study notes on topics such as topology, networks, probability, and optimization. Others are technical write-ups of modelling projects, numerical experiments, or papers that I am working through.
The emphasis is on clarity, self-contained exposition, and careful reasoning. Most posts are written for my future self, but I hope they may also be useful to other students working through similar mathematical material.

You can find my code and small projects on GitHub. I also maintain a LinkedIn profile for academic and professional updates. For questions, corrections, or academic correspondence, feel free to contact me by email.

The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text: This post is a template: it demonstrates every formatting feature these notes use — inline and display math, numbered equations, theorem/proof environments, cross-references, citations, and a runnable code cell. Copy this folder to start a new post.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
Setup
Let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, i.e. \(A^\top = A\). We write the standard inner product as \(\langle x, y\rangle = x^\top y\). Symmetry is equivalent to self-adjointness:
\[
\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle \qquad \text{for all } x,y \in \mathbb{R}^n.
\tag{1}\]
The whole theorem flows from Equation 1.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
The result

Theorem 1 (Spectral Theorem) If \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric, then there exist an orthogonal matrix \(Q\) (so \(Q^\top Q = I\)) and a real diagonal matrix \(\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\) such that \[
A = Q \Lambda Q^\top .
\tag{2}\] Equivalently, \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \(A\), and every eigenvalue is real.

We build to it with two lemmas.

Lemma 1 (Eigenvalues are real) Every eigenvalue of a real symmetric \(A\) is real.


Proof. Let \(Ax = \lambda x\) with \(x \neq 0\), allowing complex \(\lambda, x\). Using the conjugate transpose \(x^*\) and \(A^\top = A\) with real entries, \[
\lambda \,\langle x, x\rangle = x^* A x = (A x)^* x \big/ \ \cdots\ = \bar\lambda\, \langle x, x\rangle .
\] Since \(\langle x,x\rangle = \|x\|^2 > 0\), we get \(\lambda = \bar\lambda\), so \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\). \(\qquad\blacksquare\)


Lemma 2 (Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal) If \(Ax = \lambda x\) and \(Ay = \mu y\) with \(\lambda \neq \mu\), then \(\langle x, y\rangle = 0\).


Proof. By Equation 1, \[
\lambda \langle x, y\rangle = \langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle = \mu \langle x, y\rangle,
\] so \((\lambda - \mu)\langle x, y\rangle = 0\). As \(\lambda \neq \mu\), \(\langle x,y\rangle = 0\). \(\qquad\blacksquare\)


Proof (Proof of Theorem 1 (sketch)). Induct on \(n\). The base case \(n=1\) is immediate. For the step, Lemma 1 gives a real eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) with unit eigenvector \(q_1\). Its orthogonal complement \(q_1^\perp\) is \(A\)-invariant (by Equation 1), so \(A\) restricts to a symmetric operator on an \((n-1)\)-dimensional space. The inductive hypothesis supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis there; adjoining \(q_1\) yields an orthonormal eigenbasis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Collecting these vectors as columns of \(Q\) gives Equation 2. \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

A complete treatment, including the self-adjoint operator version on Hilbert spaces, is in [1]; for the numerical side see [2].

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
Numerical check
Decompositions should be tested, not trusted. We build a random symmetric matrix, diagonalize it, and confirm Equation 2 holds to machine precision.



import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 6
M = rng.standard_normal((n, n))
A = (M + M.T) / 2                      # symmetrize

eigvals, Q = np.linalg.eigh(A)         # eigh exploits symmetry
Lambda = np.diag(eigvals)

reconstruction_error = np.linalg.norm(A - Q @ Lambda @ Q.T)
orthogonality_error  = np.linalg.norm(Q.T @ Q - np.eye(n))

print(f"eigenvalues (all real): {np.round(eigvals, 4)}")
print(f"|A - Q Λ Qᵀ|  = {reconstruction_error:.2e}")
print(f"|QᵀQ - I|     = {orthogonality_error:.2e}")

eigenvalues (all real): [-2.0037 -0.988   0.2761  0.4913  1.5001  1.8151]
|A - Q Λ Qᵀ|  = 1.62e-15
|QᵀQ - I|     = 1.39e-15



Figure 1



Both residuals sit near \(10^{-15}\), confirming the decomposition numerically.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
Takeaways

Symmetry \(\Rightarrow\) self-adjointness (Equation 1) is the engine of the whole proof.
Real eigenvalues (Lemma 1) and orthogonality (Lemma 2) are the two ingredients.
In practice, call a symmetry-aware routine like eigh, not the general eig.
